blocks.text: PROJECT 2 • EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
Activity 1 • Get help safely
Mission: help a listener locate an emergency using only your words.
Set up the practice
In teams of three, use a paper phone, a pencil, two copies of a simple school map and a scenario card. One learner calls, one listens and one observes. Rotate until everyone has called.
Drill rule: use paper props only. Never dial an emergency number during practice. Do not stage a fall, make a spill, touch a classmate or try a treatment.
Scenario card • Read this aloud
“Near the main gate, beside the blue bench, a visitor has fallen. One person is on the ground. Broken glass is nearby. You are on the safe side of the gate.” These are all the facts you have.
1 • Stop at a safe place
Point to a safe spot on the map. Do not approach the glass. Alert a teacher or another nearby adult from where you are.
2 • Give the location first
The caller uses the paper phone. Say the school name, street or landmark, gate and exact spot. Keep your map hidden from the listener.
3 • Describe what you can see
Say how many people need help and mention the glass. If asked something the card does not tell you, say “I don’t know”. Listen to the next question.
4 • Test your message
The listener marks the spot on their map. Compare maps. If the marks differ, add one clearer landmark and try again. Swap roles.
In a real emergency in India, call 112 from a safe place or ask a specific person to call. If no adult is immediately available, do not delay an urgent call. Follow the dispatcher’s instructions.
MY START  Read the fictional facts. Underline the exact place and circle the visible hazard.
PARTNER TEST  Rotate caller, listener and observer. Compare the listener’s marked location with yours.
ADULT CHECK  Wait for a school-approved scenario and facts. Use paper props; never dial during practice.
Try 61 • Card 62 • Improve 63 • Check 64

PRACTICE EXAMPLE • “We need help at River School, Station Road, main gate, beside the blue bench. One visitor has fallen. There is broken glass near them. I am outside the gate.”

What I see / number of people / danger: _____________________________
Short drill log
Listener found the spot: first try / after a change
Five thinking questions
1. What kept you safe while you called for help?
2. Which landmark helped the listener find the visitor?
3. What did you see, and what would have been a guess?
4. What would you do if no adult was nearby in a real emergency?
5. Which words would you change for a visitor who does not know the school?
Privacy: use fictional people in drills. Share real emergency details with the responsible adult or dispatcher; do not post names or pictures.

MY FINISH CHECK  Tick only when your work shows it. Leave unfinished items unticked.
□ My message gives an exact location and only known facts.
□ My listener marked the place; I kept their feedback.
□ My revised message shows what I changed and why.
IF I AM STUCK  Use the sample on p. 62 for the order of information. Replace its details with the approved task facts.
TRY FIRST  If a practice card gives no injury detail, should I invent one to sound helpful?
CHECK AFTER TRYING  No. Say “I do not know”. Report what the card actually tells you.
Show the relevant record and explain one choice. My question or next step: __________________________
TEACHER REVIEW  The adult completes the assessment below. My own check is preparation, not permission or staff verification.
Prepare • 10 minutes

Confirm the school emergency plan, local address, best entrance and who is normally on duty. Draw an accessible route and choose a fictional scenario. Distinguish the practice signal from the school’s real emergency signal.
Practise • 25 minutes

Model one short call, then let teams try. Give every learner a turn initiating a message, aloud, by pointing to a communication card or through their usual communication aid. Use the listener’s map mark to test whether the message was clear.
Debrief • 10 minutes
Ask what helped the listener find the spot. Invite the school nurse, safety lead or office staff member to explain how responders are met at the gate. Use their advice to correct the class guide.
Watch for the four Cs

Critical thinking: distinguishes visible facts from guesses. Creativity: finds a clearer landmark. Collaboration: rotates roles and listens. Communication: gives a location that another person can find.
Record one observation per learner

Learner: ______________  Date: __________  Independent / prompted / next practice
Stayed clear of the hazard: ______   Alerted help: ______
Gave location and observable facts: ______   Used feedback: ______
One next step: __________________________________________________

Keep the completed call card and the listener’s marked map as evidence. Assess the student’s choices and clarity, not acting ability. A real incident ends the drill immediately; follow the school emergency plan.
Teacher reference: Government of India, Emergency Response Support System, https://112.gov.in/
Next activity: Map the adults, help points and access routes at our school.
PROJECT 2 • EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
Activity 2 • Map Your School’s Help Points
A new student knows they need an adult but does not know where to go. Make a map they can use from your classroom. Use the help-call card from Activity 1 to describe where help is needed.
1 • Choose a starting point

Mark your classroom with a star on a teacher-approved outline. Use the office or another staffed place the teacher identifies as your destination. Gather a pencil, two copies of the outline and a clipboard.
2 • Find out who can help
On a supervised walk, ask the staff member: “Who is usually here? If this room is closed, where should a student ask for help?” Label the role and the backup help point on your map.
3 • Trace the route
Walk the approved route with your teacher or trace it together on an accessible desk map. Mark each turn with an arrow. Add a fixed landmark and ask staff to confirm a step-free route if needed.
Walk only with permission. Stay out of restricted rooms and keep doors and corridors clear. This practice map does not replace the school’s emergency or evacuation plan.
MY START  Mark your classroom on the approved outline. Prepare one question about backup help.
PARTNER TEST  Test directions on paper without pointing; swap roles and note one unclear turn.
ADULT CHECK  Wait for permission and supervision before any school walk. Staff confirm routes and backups.
Steps 65–66 • Draw and verify 68 • Return to think and check 67
PROJECT 2 • EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
Test and Finish Your Map
Finished example: the arrow takes a visitor from the classroom along the corridor to the office by the blue bench. Use the real landmarks and staff roles your school confirms.
4 • Try it with a partner
Give your partner a blank outline. Read your directions without pointing. Ask them to mark the destination and trace the turns. Compare the two routes, change one unclear instruction and swap roles.
5 • Check with a staff member

Show the revised route, backup destination and accessibility notes to the teacher or office staff. Ask which entrance trained responders normally use. Only add it if staff approve; adults meet responders.

My map key: star = start; arrows = approved route; H = staffed help point. Label each room. First sketch the approved outline in pencil; then add the key and test it. Keep your first attempt with the revised map.
Short log • Start: __________  Help point / role: __________________
Keep the map for approved school use. Leave out personal phone numbers, staff schedules and security details. If the route is blocked during a real incident, follow staff instructions.
PROJECT 2 • EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
Think and Share • The Help-Point Map
1. Which landmark helped your partner choose the correct turn?
2. Where would you ask for help if your first room were closed?
3. What could make your route difficult for someone using a wheelchair?
4. What did your partner misunderstand, and how did you revise the map?
5. Which detail did a staff member confirm that you could not safely guess?
MY FINISH CHECK After drawing your map on p. 68, return here. Tick only what your work shows.
□ My map has a start, named help point, backup, arrows and a key.
□ I kept the first draft and a partner-tested revision.
□ Staff have checked the facts, or my map remains clearly a draft.
IF I AM STUCK  Use the key on p. 66. Write the room name next to H. A symbol without a key may confuse a reader.
TRY FIRST  Does my help-point map replace the school evacuation plan?
CHECK AFTER TRYING  No. It supports asking for help. Staff control emergency and evacuation procedures.
Show the relevant record and explain one choice. My question or next step: __________________________
Teacher observation • 45 minutes

Allow 10 minutes for the briefing, 15 for the supervised walk or desk mapping, 10 for the partner test and 10 for staff verification and reflection. Check the route in advance and confirm access arrangements with the school.

Every learner marks a help point and gives or tests directions. Offer large-print outlines, tactile route markers or spoken instructions. Keep the first draft and the checked map together so the improvement is visible.
Look for four actions: checks a doubtful route, devises a clear symbol, takes turns with a partner and gives directions the listener can follow.
Independent / with a prompt / needs practice: ______________________

PROJECT 2 • EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
Activity 3 • Meet the School First-Aid Kit
Our mission: investigate the kit and make a staff-checked illustrated guide

A new student spots the school first-aid box and asks, “Can anyone open it and use what is inside?” Your team has been asked to make a guide that explains where help is available and who takes responsibility.
Illustrative school visit. Observe approved items; do not practise treatment.
Wonder before you work
What makes a kit ready for use: a full box, or people who know how to look after it?
What we need
Workbook, pencil, clipboard, drawing colours and school-approved item pictures. The responsible adult provides the kit or a demonstration set. Use sealed packs for observation only.
Before we begin

Observe with the teacher and responsible staff member. Do not open sterile packs, try supplies on anyone, handle used materials or administer medicines. Trained adults decide and provide care. This is preparedness learning, not medical training or certification.

Plan: two supervised lessons of about 45 minutes. Rotate asking, observing, recording and drawing so everyone contributes. Use pictures or an adult-led classroom visit if the storage area is inaccessible.
MY START  Prepare two questions: who provides care, and who checks the kit? Find p. 72.
PARTNER TEST  Compare notes with the adult’s explanation; test whether your guide is easy to read.
ADULT CHECK  Wait for the arranged staff meeting. Adults select items; packs stay sealed and no treatment is practised.
Picture steps 70–71 • Record 72 • Draw 73 • Think 74 • Check 75
PROJECT 2 • EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
Activity 3 • Picture steps
Meet the adult • Observe • Ask before recording
1 • Meet the responsible adult

Your teacher arranges a visit with the school nurse, trained first aider or staff member responsible for the kit. Ask: “Who provides care? Who checks and restocks this kit?” The roles may belong to different people.
Check: write confirmed staff roles. Never assume that every staff member is trained.
2 • Identify approved items
The adult selects safe items or pictures to show. Match each one to its package label and sketch it in your record. Record at least four observed items; write “not shown” when necessary.
Check: examples above are not a required school-kit list. Contents follow the school’s assessed needs.
3 • Ask what each item is for
Ask: “What is its purpose? Who may use it? What should a student do?” Write a short explanation in your own words, then read it back to the adult. If unsure, write “ask adult”.
Check: describe purpose only. Do not copy treatment instructions or practise application.
PROJECT 2 • EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
Activity 3 • Picture steps
Check responsibility • Build the guide • Test and improve
4 • Find out how the kit stays ready

Ask where a student should request help, what happens if that help point is closed, and who checks the kit. Ask the adult to show how they check dates and sealed packaging. Record the school’s checking routine and how missing items are reported.
Check: never remove or discard supplies. Adults manage replacement and disposal. Leave keys, codes and private staff details out of your guide.
5 • Create your illustrated kit guide

Use the guide page to draw four items and write one purpose for each. Add the approved help point, responsible role, backup help point and one clear student safety rule. Use large labels and reusable paper where suitable.
Check: use your school’s confirmed facts. Do not include medicines or treatment directions.
6 • Test, revise and verify

Ask a partner to find the help point, responsible adult and one item purpose using only your guide. Record one difficulty. Improve the guide, then ask the responsible adult to check the information and date it.
Check: a clear-looking guide is not verified until staff have checked its facts. Use it only in the school-approved way.

Observe safe participation, accurate records and improvement

Two lessons, about 90 minutes: briefing and interview preparation 10; adult-led observation and interview 20; recording and cleanup 15; guide creation 25; partner test 10; staff check and reflection 10.

Before the visit: confirm the school kit policy, responsible staff and approved access. Keep the real kit ready for emergencies; use pictures or a separate demonstration set where needed. The adult manages all supplies and stops the activity for a real incident.

Observable action

Critical thinking: checks a doubtful label. Creativity: designs readable drawings. Communication: asks and confirms. Collaboration: shares roles and tests the guide. Green skills: reuses drawing materials; never reuses disposable care supplies.

Inclusion: offer large-print labels, item photographs, accessible seating and dictated or spoken records. Each learner contributes a practical action. Assess accuracy and judgement, not drawing skill. Obtain permission for photographs; exclude people’s medical details.

Activity 4 • Choose a Safe Response
A tabletop challenge • Notice clearly • Decide together • Communicate calmly
It is a busy school day. One team notices broken glass, another hears that a classmate feels unwell, and a third finds a corridor closed. Would the same response work in all three situations?
Your mission
Use three fictional picture cards to choose safe actions, give an accurate message and improve your team’s response. Reuse your help-call card, help-point map and kit guide from Activities 1–3.
THINK • Which part of the board helps you avoid guessing what has happened?
What we need
Workbook, pencil, four reusable paper counters, scrap-paper response cards, and your checked guide pages. The teacher provides the fictional scenario cards and school-approved help arrangements.
Safe play agreement

This is paper-based practice under teacher supervision. Do not stage illness or injury, scatter glass, block a corridor, sound an alarm, dial a number, touch a classmate or practise treatment. Students do not diagnose or give medicines. Adults take charge of care.
Plan: two 45-minute lessons. Teacher checks the scenarios and access needs first. Any real incident ends the game immediately; follow the school emergency plan.
MY START  Read cards A–C. Mark what is known and what would be a guess.
PARTNER TEST  Use the four roles on p. 80. Rotate after each round and keep observer notes.
ADULT CHECK  Wait for approved scenarios and a safety briefing. Decisions stay on paper; the teacher confirms them.
Cards 77–79 • Roles 80 • Record 81 • Think 82 • Check 83

Activity 4 • Station A — Spot the Hazard
Read the picture and facts • Choose without approaching
Fictional scene A • Broken glass beside a school drinking-water point.
THINK • Where should the students stop, and which detail must the teacher hear?
CARD FACTS: You see broken glass beside the water point. Three students are nearby. A teacher is visible at the doorway. No injury has been reported. Do not invent one.
1 • Choose and explain
Circle your choice: A. Pick up the pieces.  B. Keep clear and alert the teacher.  C. Step over the glass to inspect it.
My reason, using one visible fact: __________________________________
2 • Make a clear message
Tell the listener the location, visible hazard and who is nearby. Ask the listener to repeat the location and hazard. No one plays an injured person.
Listener repeated accurately: location □  hazard □  people nearby □
3 • Respond to the change card
Teacher reads: “The doorway teacher has gone inside.” Use your school’s checked backup help arrangement. Do not cross the glass or clean it yourself.
PROJECT 2 • EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
Activity 4 • Station B — Facts, Not Guesses
Notice a person’s need • Ask for adult help respectfully
Fictional scene B • A classmate says they feel unwell in the library.
THINK • What can you report accurately without naming an illness?
CARD FACTS: A classmate sits upright at the reading table and says, “I feel unwell.” The librarian is at the counter in the same room. You do not know the cause.
1 • Sort fact from guess
Mark F for fact or G for guess: “They say they feel unwell” ___; “They have food poisoning” ___; “The librarian is at the counter” ___.
2 • Ask for help with empathy
Write a calm message to the librarian. Give the exact place and what the classmate said. Respect their privacy; do not film, crowd around or share the incident.
A respectful sentence to the classmate: _____________________________
3 • Respond to the change card
Teacher reads: “Another student offers a tablet from their bag.” Explain your student boundary and alert the responsible adult. Do not offer medicine, food or drink as a remedy.
In real life, a sudden serious change needs immediate adult/emergency help. Do not wait to finish the worksheet.
PROJECT 2 • EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
Activity 4 • Station C — The Route Has Changed
Use your map carefully • Follow authorised directions
Fictional scene C • A corridor is closed for repairs; a teacher is nearby.
THINK • Why does a route drawn on yesterday’s map need checking today?
CARD FACTS: Your usual route to the office is blocked by a repair barrier. Debris is beyond it. A teacher is visible at an open doorway on your side of the barrier.
1 • Make a safe choice
Circle your choice: A. Move the barrier.  B. Squeeze past the debris.  C. Stay clear and ask the teacher for the approved next step.
The fact that supports my choice: _________________________________
2 • Check access before changing the map
Use your Activity 2 map. Point to the usual help point and backup. Ask the teacher which option is available now and whether it suits someone who needs step-free access. Do not invent a shortcut.
3 • Respond to the change card
Teacher reads: “A friend says a shortcut through a restricted room is faster.” Explain why speed does not make the route suitable. Record only the teacher-approved option.
This is help-seeking practice. It does not replace the school’s evacuation plan or authorise students to lead an evacuation.
PROJECT 2 • EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
Activity 4 • Run the Response Lab
Four roles • Four short rounds • Every learner contributes
THINK • How could a careful listener improve a response without giving medical advice?
4 • Choose your roles and rotate
Role
What I do
Safety spotter
Names a visible hazard and a safe choice.
Message maker
Gives location and facts; asks for adult help.
Listener
Repeats the key details and asks one clear question.
Observer
Uses the evidence checklist and suggests one improvement.
Round 1: Station A. Round 2: Station B. Round 3: Station C. Round 4: replay the response that needed the most improvement. Move each role one place after every round. Everyone tries all four roles.
5 • Place, explain and test

Draw a small four-space response board on reused paper, using the board from the opening page. Move a counter only after your team explains its choice. The teacher confirms safety decisions. A counter marks a discussion step, not an award for speed.
6 • Listen, improve and replay
The observer gives one specific suggestion. Rewrite the unclear part and replay it. Ask the teacher to confirm the revised response. Keep both attempts as evidence of learning.
Try a communication option: speak, point to a message card, use a drawing or use your usual communication aid. The listener must still show what they understood.

PROJECT 2 • EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
Activity 5 • Practise Our School Emergency Plan
An announced school drill • Adult leadership • Calm and inclusive participation
Your class can now find help, explain a location and recognise student boundaries. But can everyone follow the school’s instructions together, including someone who needs extra support?

Your mission: take part in a school-authorised, adult-led movement-and-accountability drill, record what you notice and propose one improvement. The school decides the practice arrangements using its own emergency plan.
Illustrative practice scene. Your school confirms its own route, destination and support arrangements.
THINK • Which actions in the picture show preparedness without rushing?
What we need

Workbook, pencil and your checked help guide. The teacher holds the authorised plan and attendance register. Use reusable observation cards; no student carries a real kit or emergency equipment for this activity.
Before we begin

No surprise drill, real emergency call, staged injury, smoke, alarm experiment or student-led rescue. Adults control the start, movement, headcount and finish. Follow the school’s actual instructions; different emergencies may require different actions.
Plan: two 45-minute lessons, coordinated with the school drill timetable. Record actual learning time. If permission is unavailable, complete preparation only; do not claim a drill took place.
MY START  Write your question on p. 85. Read the readiness checks before the briefing.
PARTNER TEST  After practice, compare one clear instruction and one question for staff.
ADULT CHECK  Wait for school authorisation and the adult lead. Never begin, repeat or change a drill yourself.
Briefing 85 • Steps 86 • Record 87 • Improve 88 • Think 89 • Check 90
PROJECT 2 • EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
Activity 5 • Meet the Drill Lead
1 • Ask the responsible adult before making a plan
THINK • Why must a missing-person concern go to an adult rather than a student search team?

With your teacher, meet the school safety lead or another authorised staff member. Ask who starts and ends practice, how your class is accounted for and how everyone can participate safely. Record roles, not private contact details.
Our school-confirmed briefing
Question for the adult
Confirmed information
What are we practising today?
Who leads our class?
What is the agreed practice start signal?
Where do we go / what action do we follow?
Who checks attendance?

Keep individual support arrangements and attendance details with staff. Your workbook needs only the general arrangements approved for class use.
PROJECT 2 • EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS
Activity 5 • Picture Steps
Prepare together • Follow the adult • Stay accounted for
THINK • Which step prevents someone leaving before the teacher knows everyone is accounted for?
2 • Prepare before the start

Point to the approved destination on the staff-provided plan. Confirm your role as a participant. Tell the teacher privately about any support you need. Rehearse listening to instructions at your desk.
3 • Participate in the announced drill

Start only on the authorised signal. Follow the adult’s directions at a calm pace. Keep the route clear; do not stop for belongings or take photographs. Students do not test doors, investigate hazards or choose shortcuts.
4 • Help the adult account for everyone

Stay in the place the adult assigns. Respond when asked during attendance. If you notice someone is not with the group, tell the teacher privately. Do not go looking for them or return to the building.
5 • Finish under adult direction
Wait for the authorised all-clear. Return as instructed. Complete your notes afterwards, not while walking. If you feel unsafe or distressed, tell the supervising adult immediately.
Access rule: follow the school’s agreed support plan. Students never carry or lift another person. If a route or arrangement is unsuitable, tell the adult and follow their instructions.

Activity 6 • Test and Improve Our Help Guide
Create a useful school resource • Test with readers • Verify with staff

A new student opens your team’s emergency help guide. The pictures look attractive, but one room has no label and the backup help point is difficult to find. Can a guide be trusted just because it looks finished?

Your mission: assemble your existing work, test whether another reader can use it, collect staff feedback and produce a revised, school-checked guide. Keep the first version so you can show the improvement.

Safe and responsible testing

Plan: two 45-minute lessons. Rotate organising, testing, recording and revising; each learner explains one change. This activity improves the guide, not the school’s emergency procedures.
